agent_notes: STEPBible glosses word 1 as one unit 'praise Yahweh'; I kept it as a single gloss because the packet counts it as one token (hallelu-Yah). Word 5 (ṭov) is a verbless clause in Hebrew; STEPBible's '[he is] good' is kept with the copula in brackets.
STEPBible parses 'ekhad' as feminine (HNcfsa), an oddity; the form is the normal masculine 'one'. Not reflected in the translation.

'vaya'aminu bidvarav' uses the preposition bet with the object (believed in his words), as KJV's plain 'believed his words' does not show. The tie to Ex 14:31 and 15:1 is made in the commentaries (Meiri, Malbim, Ibn Ezra) and is cited, not invented.

The five English versions split on מהרו: KJV/ASV/Webster fold it into an adverb ('soon forgot'), YLT keeps the verb ('have hasted—forgotten'), BBE paraphrases. I kept the two finite verbs in the literal layer ('they hurried, they forgot') as the Hebrew has asyndeton, and let the dramatic layer carry the adverbial sense.
STEPBible glosses חכו as 'they waited'. Kept, but the sense is 'waited for, hoped for' (Metzudat Zion cites Zeph 3:8); the gloss includes the object.

רזון: KJV 'leanness', BBE 'wasting disease'. Both are lexically possible; context (Num 11:33 plague while the meat was still in their teeth) favours a wasting or destruction, and the ancient commentators split between 'death' (Ibn Ezra, Radak) and literal thinning (Metzudat David). I kept 'wasting' in the literal layer and left the ambiguity in the commentary.

STEPBible gives ויקנאו 'were envious'. The commentators (Radak, Meiri, Rashi) discuss the lamed after קנא as standing for bet ('envied Moses'), or as a verb of provoking; I rendered 'they were jealous of Moses', following the straightforward reading, and recorded the lamed as an open question in the note.

The verb forms are imperfect (תפתח) then wayyiqtol. Ibn Ezra and Radak read the imperfect as a past; I render all in the past tense. The Psalm names only Dathan and Abiram and omits Korah (Num 16); Rashi and Radak offer reasons, which I cite.

history.note: [consider] Put the literal layer in the past ('They made a calf at Horeb, and they bowed down…'), as the glosses and v.17-18 have it. (PS.106.19: "יַעֲשׂוּ־עֵגֶל בְּחֹרֵב וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲווּ"; Radak: "עתיד במקום עבר".)

agent_notes: Verb 'yemallel' (H4448A) is rare (Job 8:2; Ps 106:2; Gen 21:7 mille). Radak and Metzudat Zion tie it to 'speech, word' (milla); I follow that. The second clause 'yashmia' is read as a continued question, as Radak notes ('the one who asks stands for two').

כבודם (their glory) is the Masoretic text; the commentators read it as God's glory (Metzudat David: 'the glory of the Place'). Compare Jer 2:11, which I mention only as a parallel in my own reading, so no source is given.
STEPBible tags חם with entity loc.egypt, which is correct as metonymy for Egypt (Radak: Ham is the father of Mizraim).

Reviewer request applied: the commentary no longer says the word 'normally' belongs to David. It says the psalm used בְּחִירֶיךָ for all Israel in v.5 and here gives בְּחִירוֹ to one man, Moses, who stands for them; Ps 89:4 (David) is kept only as a parallel.

history.note: [should_fix] Drop 'normally gives to David'. Say instead that the psalm used the word for Israel as a whole in v.5 and here gives it to one man, Moses, who stands for them. Ps 89:4 (David) can stay as a parallel. (PS.106.5: "לִרְאוֹת בְּטוֹבַת בְּחִירֶיךָ" ('your chosen ones', Israel); PS.106.23: "מֹשֶׁה בְחִירוֹ".)

agent_notes: וימאסו בארץ חמדה: YLT 'kick against' is a loose rendering; מאס is 'reject, spurn'. 'Land of desire' is literal (חמדה, 'a desirable thing'); I kept 'desired land' in the literal layer.

history.note: [consider] Leave the 'obey' sense unsourced, or report Metzudat David's gloss as 'did not believe'. (Metzudat David on 106:25: "לא שמעו. לא האמינו בקול דברו".)

agent_notes: Hebrew 'lifted his hand to them' is the oath gesture (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Targum all read it so; ASV 'sware', BBE 'made an oath'); KJV keeps the idiom but adds 'against', which turns an oath into a blow. The literal layer keeps 'lifted his hand' and the dramatic layer lets the oath show. The Ezekiel 20 parallel is cited by Radak, not by me.

The verb is the same הפיל as in verse 26 ('make fall'), then זרה 'scatter'. The KJV 'overthrow' hides the repetition; I repeated 'make fall' in the literal layer. I did not source any textual-variant claim for this verse.

'Sacrifices of the dead' is disputed: lifeless idols (Metzudat David, Radak, Ibn Ezra: sacrifices to their gods) or offerings to dead spirits. I kept the Hebrew phrase open in the literal layer and named both readings in the commentary without choosing.

The plural 'shomerei' (those who keep) shifts to the singular 'oseh' (one who does); I kept the shift visible in the literal layer and did not harmonise as KJV's 'they ... and he' partly does. Some read the singular as a distributive.

history.note: [consider] Use 'Happy [are]' or 'Oh the happiness of' in the literal layer, to match the gloss and the commentary. (PS.106.3: "אַשְׁרֵי שֹׁמְרֵי מִשְׁפָּט".)

agent_notes: וַיְפַלֵּל (piel of פלל) splits the versions: KJV/ASV/YLT 'executed judgment' (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion: from פְּלִילִים), BBE and the Targum 'prayed' (צלי). I chose 'mediated' for the gloss and 'intervened as judge' in the literal layer, and put the prayer reading in the commentary. The spear of Numbers 25 is not in the verse; the dramatic layer does not add it.

history.note: [consider] Say 'the medieval commentators in the packet' or name the Targum as the exception. (Targum on 106:30: "וְקָם פִּינְחָס וְצַלֵי".)

agent_notes: Reviewer request applied: הִמְרוּ is 'rebelled against' in the literal layer and the gloss, as in v.7 (וַיַּמְרוּ) and v.43 (יַמְרוּ). BBE's 'made bitter' appears only as an alternative. The note no longer says Radak links the root to bitterness. The subject of הִמְרוּ and the owner of רוּחוֹ are both disputed (Israel vs. Moses and Aaron; God's spirit vs. Moses' spirit), so the commentary gives each reading to the commentator who holds it.

The five English versions split on רוּחוֹ and on who speaks rashly. KJV, ASV and Webster leave 'his' open; the Hebrew leaves it open too. I kept 'his' in the literal layer. The dramatic layer follows the reading that Moses is the one who spoke rashly, which matches Num 20:10 and the traditional reading, and the commentary says the other reading exists.

agent_notes: Reviewer request addressed: the earlier claim that this verse repeats the word of v.29 is removed (v.29 has מעלליהם, this verse מעשיהם). The commentary now points forward to v.39, where מעשיהם and מעלליהם stand together.

The five English versions agree on 'mingled/mixed' and 'learned their works'; BBE's 'joined to' flattens the hithpael of ערב. I kept 'mixed themselves', reflexive, as the literal layer. Cited Radak only for the point he makes in the packet (living among them, hence learning); Ibn Ezra's comment is too terse in the packet to rest a claim on.

history.note: [blocker] Remove the claim that v.35 repeats the word of v.29. If you keep an echo, point to v.39, where מעשיהם comes back next to מעלליהם and the nations' deeds have become Israel's own. agent_notes: עצבים 'idols' is read as a contemptuous pun on עצב 'pain, hurt' (Ibn Ezra: a name of disgrace; Metzudat Zion: the idol grieves its worshippers). The derivation is the commentators' and a standard lexicon point I am fairly, not fully, sure of, so I left lexicon sources out.

שֵׁדִים (shedim) occurs only here and in Deut 32:17. I kept 'demons' in the dramatic layer and the transliterated 'shedim' in the literal layer, since the word is a loanword (cf. Akkadian šēdu, a protective spirit that could also be hostile) and 'demons' carries later Christian freight. YLT's 'destroyers' reads it as from שׁוד; Ibn Ezra mentions this derivation (ישוד צהרים) as one opinion.

history.note: [consider] Cite lexicons the same way across the chapter. Either leave them out of `sources` and mark the claim as your own, or keep them consistently. (PS.106.37 packet commentaries: only Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David and the Targum.)

agent_notes: The Targum's 'with sins of killing' (בחובין דקטול) for בדמים is not followed; I read the plural דָּמִים as 'bloodshed', the usual sense of plural 'blood' for violence. Metzudat Zion's gloss of ותחנף as 'was made guilty' is cited for the sense of pollution; the verb is a Qal of חנף, 'was polluted/profaned', and echoes Num 35:33 (same root for land defiled by blood), which I mention in the commentary as my own observation.

STEPBible tags בְמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם with a Ketiv variant (4639K). I glossed the text as it stands. 'Became unclean' (Qal of טמא, not a passive) is kept literal: the verb is active/stative, which KJV 'were defiled' flattens into a passive.

The speaker's 'I' is disputed: Radak and Metzudat David read the psalmist for himself, Radak also reads it as the voice of the exiles. I kept 'me' and did not decide whose voice it is. 'birtzon amekha' is ambiguous: 'with the favour you show your people' (Rashi: 'when you are pleased with your people') or 'when your people find favour'. Targum has 'with good favour among your people'.

וַיָּמֹכּוּ: STEPBible takes it from מכך (H4355), 'sank'; Ibn Ezra and Meiri also relate it to מוך (Lev 25:25, 'your brother becomes poor'). Either way the sense is 'brought low'. I glossed 'sank' in the literal layer and 'brought low' in the dramatic. For ימרו בעצתם the five English versions split ('provoked with counsel' vs 'rebelled in counsel'); I chose 'rebelled', with עצה as the instrument or sphere of rebellion (their own plans), as Metzudat David and Malbim read it.

בַּצַּר לָהֶם is literally 'in the distress to them'; STEPBible's gloss 'when <the> it was distress' is awkward, so I glossed 'in [their] distress'. Whether וַיַּרְא means 'saw' or 'looked on with favour' is a judgment call; I keep 'saw' and let the dramatic layer carry the sympathy.
Ketiv חסדו (singular) / Qere חסדיו (plural). I glossed the reading (plural). The Rashi and Ibn Ezra comments on which covenant (Abraham's or Sinai's) are summarized rather than quoted at length.

Reviewer request addressed: the commentary now says the 'we' is not new. It returned from the confession of v.6 (ḥaṭanu 'im-avotenu, 'we have sinned with our fathers') and has turned from confessing to asking. Opening rewritten accordingly.

Gloss 10 lehishtabeach: STEPBible has 'to boast'. I kept 'to glory' (Hithpael of shbh), since the object is praise of God, not self-praise; Metzudat David reads it as the people praising themselves for being chosen, which I note but do not follow. The five English versions split between 'triumph' (KJV, ASV, Webster), 'glory' (YLT, BBE).
Gloss 5-6 min hagoyim: the Hebrew is 'from the nations' without 'among'; KJV 'from among the heathen' adds a word and the loaded 'heathen'.

history.note: [blocker] Rewrite the opening: the 'we' of the confession in v.6 comes back here, and it now asks for something (save us, gather us) instead of confessing. Don't say it appears for the first time. (PS.106.6: "חָטָאנוּ עִם־אֲבוֹתֵינוּ" ('we have sinned with our fathers'); PS.106.7: "אֲבוֹתֵינוּ בְמִצְרַיִם".)

agent_notes: Rashi's citation of Sanhedrin 92a for 'from this world to the world to come' is taken from the packet as given. The verb וְאָמַר is perfect with waw (translated as a jussive/future); YLT takes it as past, KJV/ASV as a wish. I follow the wish reading, as most modern versions and Radak ('and then shall be said') do. Whether הַלְלוּ־יָהּ belongs to v.48 or opens Psalm 107 is a manuscript and editorial question; the Hebrew text here puts it at the end of the verse.

'lehithallel' (Hithpael of halal) is glossed 'to boast / to glory'; the 'praise' sense is in the verb root but the reflexive means to make oneself praised or to boast. Radak and Meiri mention 'rejoice' (hillulim) as an alternative; I kept 'boast'.

'hi'evinu' is glossed 'we have done wrong' per STEPBible; HALOT/BDB read the root 'avah as 'to bend, twist', hence 'we have acted perversely'. The three verbs are intentionally a rising triad (sin, twist, wickedness); Malbim reads them as a graded escalation, which is his own homiletic reading and is not claimed here.

history.note: [consider] Attribute the escalation to Malbim in the commentary, or soften it to 'three verbs for sin'. (Malbim on 106:6: "שהם חטאו מצד התאוה או השגגה … ואנחנו העוינו מצד עוות השכל … והרשענו במזיד".)

agent_notes: The five English versions split on 'hiskilu' (understood / considered wisely / gave thought). I chose 'gave heed to / took in' in the dramatic layer and 'did not consider' in the literal layer; the Hiphil of sakhal means to act with insight, not merely to know. 'al-yam beyam-suf' has a doubled 'yam': 'at sea, at the Sea of Reeds'. Meiri explains the repetition as hyperbole (they rebelled even inside the sea); I leave that out of the translation and cite it. 'Suf' means reeds; the packet's own gloss agrees.

history.note: [consider] Rephrase: 'at the sea' is repeated and then named, 'at the Sea of Reeds'. Meiri takes the second phrase as explaining the first. (PS.106.7: "עַל־יָם בְּיַם־סוּף"; Meiri: "ובים סוף הוא פי׳ על ים".)

agent_notes: 'tehomot' (deeps) is plural; 'kamidbar' with the article means 'like the wilderness / like the steppe', not 'like a wilderness'. Isa 63:13 uses the same phrase of the same event; I mention it as a parallel I am sure of. I did not source Malbim's claim about the seabed rising.

«Аллилуия» оставлено как в Синодальном переводе; в буквальном слое — «Хвалите-Йах!», чтобы был виден краткий вид божественного имени внутри слова. «Милость» Синодального для хесед в драматическом слое заменена на «верность» и «неизменная любовь», в комментарии объяснено почему.
Синодальное «увлеклись похотью» потеряло повтор глагола и однокоренного существительного; в литеральном слое повтор сохранён («возжелали желанием»).

history.note: [should_fix] Quote the Synodal as «увлеклись похотью в пустыне» and say that it, like the KJV 'lusted exceedingly', loses the verb-plus-cognate-noun repetition. (PS.106.14: וַיִּתְאַוּוּ תַאֲוָה; ru commentary: «Синодальное „вожделели вожделения“ передаёт повтор».)

agent_notes: רָזוֹן: в Синодальном «и послал в души их истощение» — то же понимание; в комментарии отмечено, что Синодальный здесь выбирает «истощение», а «душа» у нефеш — тело, горло, жажда.

agent_notes: קְדוֹשׁ יְהוָה: в Синодальном «святого Господня»; в буквальном слое «святой Господень» (YHWH сохранено как YHWH), в драматическом — «посвящённый Господу», чтобы не потерять смысл статуса, а не личного благочестия.
Он (On) бен Пелет назван по Синодальному Чис 16:1: «Авнан, сын Фалефа».

agent_notes: Хорив и Дафан/Авирон — формы Синодального перевода; «израильтяне» в тексте не названы, подлежащее — «они».
Я сохранил глагол обмена («променяли/обменяли») и сарказм последних двух слов.

יַם־סוּף переведён в буквальном слое как «море Тростниковое», в драматическом и в комментарии — «Чермное море» не используется как перевод, но упомянуто: Синодальный перевод имеет «Чермное море» (как и KJV «Red sea»), поэтому в комментарии это сказано прямо.

По просьбе рецензента: в драматическом слое и в комментарии — синодальное «Ваал-Фегор»; в буквальном слое сохранено «Ваалу Пеора» (еврейское בעל פעור, «Ваал Пеора»), чтобы передать конструкцию с родительным падежом. Синодальный перевод отнесён к прочтению «бездушным», а не к буквальному.

«Язычники» в Синодальном; в комментарии оговорено, что иврит говорит просто גּוֹיִם, «народы».
Игра עצבים («скорби, болезненные») передана в драматическом слое: «идолов скорби»; в комментарии объяснено.
